name: Country dance

narrator.name: The Atlas narrator
narrator.voice: warm, unhurried, curious; a documentary voice that never oversells; speaks the dance's own words (names, counts) clearly
narrator.rule: The narrator only says what the profile says. Every sentence can be traced to a section, a claim or the music/movement DNA.
narrator.identity: one narrator for the whole atlas: the same face and animation everywhere; a native-speaker voice of the same character per language (studio-grade); the viewer chooses the language
narrator.wardrobe: in each episode the narrator wears the traditional apparel associated with the dance, reconstructed with meticulous care from the profile's costume notes and the licensed images — genuine and respectful, never a caricature; sacred, ceremonial or restricted attire is never worn (the narrator stays in neutral dress with a respectful nod in colour and fabric); the pack's visual_brief.wardrobe says which
narrator.languages: master narration in English; translations per language in episodes/i18n/<lang>/<slug>.json with the same scene structure (pipeline/translate.py); names, places and counts are never translated

instructor.persona: A knowledgeable dance historian or experienced caller.
instructor.rule: counts out loud; demonstrates front and back; three slow repetitions before tempo; one correction at a time

scenes.title: Where and when
narration: Country dance began to influence courtly dance in the 15th century and became particularly popular at the court of Elizabeth I. John Playford’s 1651 publication, The English Dancing Master, established a practical monopoly on dance manuals for decades.
The form was introduced to the French court in 1684, where it was adapted into the contredanse.
A revival occurred in the early 20th century led by Cecil Sharp and Mary Neal.
on_screen: Map: United Kingdom · Europe
Image 1 with attribution

scenes.title: When it is danced
narration: Country dance is intended for general social participation.
It was historically used as a refreshing finale to more formal, stately dances like the minuet.
Today it is a living tradition.

scenes.title: Watch it
narration: Dancers form sets, most commonly longways lines or squares.
The dance consists of a series of figures linked together to fit the music.
Dancers progress through the set to interact with different partners.
Watch for Circle Left, Strip the Willow.
on_screen: Hero video full screen, 30–45 s (vOKpizJ_9RE)
Captions name each signature move as it appears
Formation: longways lines or squares

scenes.title: Listen
narration: The most common musical forms are 32-bar jigs and reels, typically written in 2/4 or 6/8 time.
Historically, the music was traditional folk music, though modern bands experiment with various genres.
Listen for the traditional folk instruments.
The pulse is 2/4 or 6/8.
Bright and rhythmic music, typically structured in 32-bar phrases, designed to support the timing of the dance figures.

scenes.title: The people
narration: John Playford, Raoul Auger Feuillet, Cecil Sharp, Mary Neal, Thomas Wilson.
Contra dance (United States), Scottish country dance, Irish set dance, Contradanza (Latin America), Engelska (Scandinavia).
Influenced by Renaissance courtly dance and early styles like the morris dance.

music_brief.purpose: original soundtrack faithful to the tradition, with documented commercial reuse rights and no recurring royalties
music_brief.rights_rule: A composition brief does not clear an output. Record the provider/model/version, terms and date, input rights, output licence, restrictions and review before release.
music_brief.sound_description: Bright and rhythmic music, typically structured in 32-bar phrases, designed to support the timing of the dance figures.
music_brief.prompt: Original instrumental composition in the musical world of Country dance (United Kingdom). Meter 2/4 or 6/8. Instruments: traditional folk instruments. Mood: bright, rhythmic, simple. It should sound like this: Bright and rhythmic music, typically structured in 32-bar phrases, designed to support the timing of the dance figures. New melody, new arrangement: do not quote or imitate any specific recorded song; keep the idiom, the instruments, the pulse and the proportions.

tracks.use: chapters: dance it to the music

rules: Original composition only — no sampling, no melody of any existing recording, no lyrics from any song.
Traditional public-domain tunes may be used only when the profile names them and a public-domain source is on file; otherwise compose new material in the idiom.
Keep the proportions true: the meter, the tempo range and the instrument roles the sources describe.
Label every generated track with the tool, the date and this brief, so provenance is always clear.
